title: Governor of Georgia

context.text: Open seat: Republican Gov. Brian Kemp cannot seek a third consecutive term.

Republican primary: businessman Rick Jackson and Lt. Gov. Burt Jones led the May 19 first round but neither reached 50 percent, forcing a June 16 runoff, which Jackson won. President Trump had endorsed Jones before the runoff and endorsed Jackson in July.
Democratic primary: former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms won the May nomination without a runoff against six other candidates.

Libertarian Chase Oliver, the 2024 Libertarian presidential nominee, was announced by the Libertarian Party of Georgia on March 6 as having filed paperwork to run for governor. The party had lost automatic ballot access and, per WABE (July 10), turned in only a few hundred of the more than 70,000 petition signatures needed (the party's own March release put the requirement at over 80,000), and WABE reported that Libertarians will not appear on the November ballot, though write-in candidacies remain possible. Wikipedia lists Oliver as withdrawn. WSB-TV's October 14 statewide list nevertheless names Oliver as the Libertarian candidate. These sources conflict, and no official ballot was available to settle it. This guide lists the two nominees.

candidates.name: Rick Jackson
candidates.ballotNote: Won the Republican nomination in the June 16 runoff over Lt. Gov. Burt Jones.

summary.text: Rick Jackson is a health care staffing executive and first-time candidate who founded Jackson Healthcare. He won the Republican nomination in a June runoff after spending more than $100 million of his own money in the primary campaign. He proposes cutting the state income tax in half within four years, limiting property-tax increases, and expanding support for sheriffs and law enforcement.

background.text: Grew up in Atlanta, including in the Techwood Homes public housing community, and spent time in five foster homes; attended David Lipscomb College but did not finish.
Bought the staffing company where he worked in 1976 and built it into Jackson Healthcare, an Alpharetta-based medical staffing firm that reports annual revenue above $3 billion.
Backed a 2022 Georgia law providing tax credits for donations supporting young people leaving foster care.

priorities.text: Cutting the state income tax in half within four years and working toward eliminating it within eight, freezing increases in home valuations, and ending state income taxes on tips.
Making third-grade reading proficiency a central education priority and supporting higher teacher pay.
More resources and personnel for sheriffs and tougher enforcement against violent crime.

positions.summary: Supports Georgia's existing abortion law, including its exceptions for rape, incest and the mother's life.
Supports closer cooperation with the Trump administration on immigration enforcement and has pledged to make deporting unauthorized immigrants who break the law a priority.
Reported in August as opposing full Medicaid expansion; at the October 6 debate said he supports expanding Medicaid provided it does not jeopardize $4.5 billion in existing federal funding.
Supports additional resources and personnel for sheriffs; his campaign announced endorsements from 104 Georgia sheriffs.
Has endorsed Georgia's participation in the federal tax credit program supporting donations for private school scholarships.

candidates.name: Keisha Lance Bottoms
candidates.ballotNote: Won the Democratic primary in May without a runoff.

summary.text: Keisha Lance Bottoms is a former Atlanta mayor and Biden White House official. She is campaigning on expanding Medicaid, lowering driving costs, a statewide affordable-housing trust fund, and repealing Georgia's abortion restrictions.

background.text: Earned a bachelor's degree from Florida A&M University and a law degree from Georgia State University; worked as an attorney and magistrate judge.
Elected to the Atlanta City Council in 2009 and re-elected in 2013, representing District 11.
Served as Atlanta's 60th mayor from 2018 to 2022, then as director of the White House Office of Public Engagement in the Biden administration.

priorities.text: Expanding Medicaid, which she has described as a priority for the start of her administration, and criticizing the limited Georgia Pathways program.
Lowering driving costs by eliminating the state's 2.25% tax on auto insurance premiums and cutting the state gasoline tax to 28 cents a gallon.
Creating a statewide affordable-housing trust fund, raising the minimum wage to $15 an hour, and making community and technical colleges tuition-free.

positions.summary: Supports repealing Georgia's abortion restrictions and restoring protections consistent with the Roe v. Wade standard.
Has advocated raising Georgia's minimum wage to $15 an hour.

record.text: As mayor, decided to stop allowing Immigration and Customs Enforcement to use Atlanta's jail, as she cited in a Democratic primary debate.
In 2021, her mayoral campaign agreed to pay a $37,000 state ethics fine for campaign finance violations connected to the 2017 election, including contributions above legal limits.

researchNotes: Ballotpedia was blocked in this environment, so the slate was assembled from news coverage (FOX 5 Atlanta, WSB-TV, WABE) and Wikipedia. Georgia elects its lieutenant governor separately, so there are no running mates. Chase Oliver (Libertarian) is not included: WABE (July 10) reports Libertarians failed the petition drive and will not be on the ballot, and Wikipedia lists him as withdrawn; only WSB-TV's Oct 14 list still names him (it appears to repeat the March qualifying list). Pass 2: Georgia's MVP/sample-ballot pages are login-gated or 403, results.sos.ga.gov has no 2026 general-election data yet, and no county sample ballot PDF could be found, so this remains unresolved by an official source; the guide follows WABE, which reports the petition drive failed. The official Secretary of State candidate list (results.sos.ga.gov is script-rendered; mvp.sos.ga.gov returned 403) could not be loaded, so this is a news-only slate check. Checked 2026-10-19. Candidate positions come from FOX 5 Atlanta's October 2026 profiles, which cite AJC reporting; the profiles' underlying articles were not individually opened. Jackson has not held public office, so he has no official record. Bottoms' mayoral record is limited to items reported in the FOX 5 profile.
